title: Singly linked list: deleting nodes & selection sort
overview: This module finishes the basic singly linked list toolkit: removing the head, the tail and a node at any index, then sorting the list with selection sort by swapping values. The practice day uses those pieces to compare list sizes, find the maximum and sort in either order. Once these moves are in your fingers, every later linked-list problem is a remix of them.

concepts.explain: To remove a node you first save a pointer to it, then make the node before it skip over it, and only then call `delete`. If you delete first, you lose the link you still need.
In a singly list you can only change the `next` of the node *before* the target. So the walk to delete index `idx` stops at index `idx-1` (the loop runs `i = 1 .. idx-1`).
Deleting the head changes which node `head` points to. `Node* &head` lets the function change the caller's variable; with a plain `Node* head` the change is lost.
Even if you keep a `tail` pointer, you must walk from the head to find the node just before the tail, because there is no backward link.

For each position `i`, compare it with every later position `j` and swap whenever the later value is smaller. After pass `i`, position `i` holds the smallest remaining value. Two nested loops, so O(n²).
concepts.snippet: for i in 0..n-2: for j in i+1..n-1: if a[j] < a[i]: swap

concepts.term: Sort a list by swapping values
concepts.explain: On a linked list, the two loop variables are node pointers (`i`, `j`) instead of indexes. We swap `i->val` and `j->val`; the nodes themselves never move, which keeps the code short.
concepts.snippet:
for(Node* i=head; i->next; i=i->next)
  for(Node* j=i->next; j; j=j->next)

concepts.explain: Insert at head O(1); insert at tail O(1) with a tail pointer (O(n) without); delete head O(1); delete tail or any index O(n); print O(n); selection sort O(n²).

files.title: Delete the head node
files.what: Reads values until `-1` into a list, prints it, removes the first node with `delete_head`, and prints again.
steps: `insert_at_tail` adds each value in O(1) because `tail` is remembered.
`delete_head` saves the old head in `deleteNode`.
It moves `head` one step forward: `head = head->next`.
Finally `delete deleteNode` frees the old first node.
`head` is taken by reference, so `main` sees the new head.
files.complexity: Time O(1) for the delete · Space O(1)
files.input_note: Values of the list, ended by -1.
files.output_note: The first four lines are the list before (10 20 30 40); the last three are after the delete (20 30 40) — 10 is gone.
files.watch_out: There is no check for an empty list: calling `delete_head` when `head` is `NULL` crashes. Add `if(head == NULL) return;` first.

check.a: The function changes where `head` points; without the reference only a local copy would change and `main` would still point at the freed node.

files.title: Delete the head node (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed copy of `delete_head.cpp`; the code is the same.
steps: Same logic: save the head, move `head` forward, free the saved node.

check.q: After deleting the head of `5 -> 6 -> 7`, what does `head->val` print?

files.title: Delete the node at an index
files.what: Builds a list, then removes the node at index 2 (0-based) with `delete_at_any_position` by making its previous node skip it.
steps: `tmp` starts at `head` and the loop `for(i=1; i<idx; i++)` moves it to index `idx-1`.
With `idx = 2`, `tmp` ends on the node with value 20 (index 1).
`deleteNode = tmp->next` remembers the node at index 2 (value 30).
`tmp->next = tmp->next->next` links 20 straight to 40.
`delete deleteNode` frees 30.
files.complexity: Time O(idx) → O(n) worst case · Space O(1)
files.input_note: List values ended by -1; the index 2 is fixed in the code.
files.output_note: First block: 10 20 30 40 50. Second block: 10 20 40 50 — the value at index 2 (30) was removed.
files.watch_out: It does not handle `idx = 0` (that needs `delete_head`) or an index past the end (`tmp->next` becomes `NULL` and `tmp->next->next` crashes). Check `idx` against the list size first.

check.q: To delete index 4, on which index does `tmp` stop?
check.a: Index 3 — the node just before the one being deleted.

files.title: Delete at an index (practice copy)
files.what: Same program; the only change is that `delete_at_any_position` takes `head` by reference (`Node* &head`).
steps: Identical walk-and-skip logic. The reference is harmless here but would matter if the function also handled index 0.
files.output_note: Same result as the original: 30 disappears from the second block.

check.q: Is the reference on `head` needed to delete index 2?
check.a: No — `head` itself does not change; it only becomes necessary when deleting index 0.

files.title: Delete the tail node
files.what: Shows two ways to remove the last node: `delete_tail` walks to the node before `tail`, and `delete_tail2` uses a known index. The program does not compile because of the call in `main`.
steps: `delete_tail` saves `tail` in `deleteNode`.
`tmp` walks from `head` until `tmp->next == tail`, i.e. the second-last node.
It cuts the link with `tmp->next = NULL` and moves `tail = tmp`.
Then it frees the old tail.
`delete_tail2` does the same using index `size-1`, and also updates `tail`.
files.output_note: No output: the compiler stops with "too few arguments to function delete_tail".
files.watch_out: `main` calls `delete_tail(head);` but the function needs two arguments. Fix: `delete_tail(head, tail);`. Also, with a one-node list the `while` never finds a node before `tail` and crashes — handle `head == tail` separately.

check.q: Why is deleting the tail O(n) even though we keep a `tail` pointer?
check.a: We must update the second-last node's `next`, and a singly list can only reach it by walking from the head.

files.title: Delete the tail (practice copy)
files.what: A re-typed version with the function renamed to `delete_at_tail`; it has typing mistakes and does not compile.
steps: Same idea: walk to the node before `tail`, cut the link, move `tail`, free the old tail.
`delete_tail2` here forgets `delete deleteNode`, so the removed node leaks memory.
files.output_note: No output: compile errors (missing `;` and an unknown function name).
files.watch_out: Two errors: `tmp = tmp->next` is missing its `;`, and `main` calls `delete_tail(head)` although the function is now `delete_at_tail(head, tail)`. Fix both lines.

check.q: What goes wrong if you forget `delete deleteNode`?
check.a: The node is unlinked but its memory is never freed — a memory leak.

files.title: Selection sort on an array
files.what: Reads `n` numbers and sorts them in ascending order with the swap-based selection sort, as a warm-up for sorting a linked list.
steps: The outer loop fixes position `i` from 0 to `n-2`.
The inner loop checks every `j` after `i`.
If `arr[j] < arr[i]`, the two are swapped, so `arr[i]` keeps the smallest value seen so far.
After the inner loop, position `i` is final.
The sorted array is printed on one line.

check.q: After the first outer pass on `5 2 9 1 7`, what is in `arr[0]`?
check.a: 1, the minimum of the whole array.

files.title: Selection sort on an array (practice copy)
files.what: Same program, but with a typo in the input loop, so it does not compile.
steps: Same nested-loop selection sort.
files.output_note: No output: compile error "no match for operator>".
files.watch_out: `cin > arr[i];` uses a single `>`. It must be `cin >> arr[i];`.

files.title: Selection sort on a linked list
files.what: Sorts a singly linked list in ascending order by running selection sort with two node pointers and swapping the values.
steps: `i` starts at `head` and stops at the last-but-one node (`i->next != NULL`).
`j` starts at `i->next` and runs to the end (`j != NULL`).
If `i->val > j->val`, `swap(i->val, j->val)`.
Links are never changed — only the numbers inside the nodes move.
The list is printed before and after sorting.
files.output_note: First four lines: the original order 40 10 30 20. Last four: 10 20 30 40.
files.watch_out: `i->next != NULL` crashes on an empty list (`head` is `NULL`). Check `head` first.

check.q: Why is `i`'s loop condition `i->next != NULL` and not `i != NULL`?
check.a: The last node has nothing after it to compare with, so the outer loop can stop one node early.

steps: Same two-pointer selection sort with value swaps.

files.title: Do two lists have the same size?
files.what: Reads two lists (each ended by `-1`), counts their nodes with `get_size`, and prints YES if the counts match, otherwise NO.
steps: The first `while` loop builds list 1 with `head`/`tail`.
`get_size` walks the list and counts nodes.
The second loop builds list 2 with `head2`/`tail2`.
Compare `size_1` and `size_2` and print YES or NO.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.input_note: Two lines, each a list ended by -1.
files.output_note: `YES` — both lists hold 3 values (the values themselves do not matter).

check.a: Yes — only the sizes are compared.

files.title: Same size check (practice copy)
files.what: Same program, but a constructor typo leaves `next` holding garbage, so counting never ends.
steps: Same logic: build both lists, count, compare.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.output_note: The run times out (or may crash): `get_size` follows a garbage `next` pointer instead of stopping at `NULL`. The expected answer would be `NO`.
files.watch_out: The constructor says `this->next = next;` — there is no parameter called `next`, so the member is assigned to itself and stays uninitialised. Fix: `this->next = NULL;`.

check.q: Why must a new node's `next` be set to `NULL`?
check.a: Loops stop when they reach `NULL`; an uninitialised pointer sends them into random memory.

files.title: Print a list in reverse (attempt)
files.what: The task was to print the list in reverse, but the code actually sorts it in ascending order with selection sort.
steps: Build the list with `insert_at_tail` and print it.
`sort_linked_list` runs the usual two-pointer selection sort.
Print the list again — it is now sorted, not reversed.
files.output_note: The first six lines are the input order; the last six are 1 2 4 5 6 8 — sorted. A true reverse would be 1 2 6 8 4 5.
files.watch_out: Sorting is not reversing. For a reverse print use recursion: `print_reverse(node->next)` first, then print `node->val` (see Module 10's `print_reverse`).

check.q: For `3 1 2`, what are the sorted order and the reversed order?

files.title: Maximum value in a list
files.what: Walks the list once, keeping the largest value seen, and prints it.
steps: If the list is empty, `find_max` returns -1.
`max` starts at `INT_MIN`, smaller than any real value.
For each node, if `tmp->val > max`, update `max`.
Return and print `max`.
files.watch_out: The code uses `INT_MIN` without including `<climits>`; it compiles here only because another header pulls it in.

check.a: If every value is negative, starting at 0 would give the wrong answer 0.

files.title: Maximum value (practice copy)
files.what: Identical re-typing of the maximum finder.
steps: Same single pass with a running `max`.

check.q: How would you instead start `max` without `INT_MIN`?
check.a: Start with `max = head->val` (after checking the list is not empty).

files.title: Sort a list in descending order (buggy)
files.what: Selection sort with the comparison flipped (`<`) to get descending order, but the inner loop never advances.
steps: Outer pointer `i` walks the list; inner pointer `j` should walk from `i->next` to the end.
If `i->val < j->val`, swap, so bigger values move to the front.
Print the list on one line.
files.complexity: Time O(n²) once fixed · Space O(1)
files.output_note: The run times out with no output: the inner loop spins forever. Once fixed it prints `40 30 20 10`.
files.watch_out: The inner loop update is `j->next` (reads a value and throws it away) instead of `j = j->next`, so `j` never moves. Fix the update to `j = j->next`.

check.q: What is the only difference between the ascending and descending selection sort?
check.a: The comparison: `>` swaps for ascending, `<` swaps for descending.

files.what: Re-typed version: the loop update is now correct, but `j` is never declared, so it does not compile.
steps: Same descending selection sort.
files.output_note: No output: compile error "'j' was not declared in this scope".
files.watch_out: Write `for(Node* j = i->next; j != NULL; j = j->next)` — the type `Node*` is missing.

check.q: After the fix, what does `1 4 5 2 7 -1` print?

files.title: Sort a list in ascending order (buggy)
files.what: Ascending selection sort on a linked list with the same frozen inner loop as the descending version.
steps: `i` walks the list; `j` should scan the nodes after `i`.
If `i->val > j->val`, swap the values.
Print the sorted list on one line.
files.complexity: Time O(n²) once fixed · Space O(1)
files.output_note: Times out with no output. With the fix it prints `10 20 30 40`.
files.watch_out: Inner loop update `j->next` must be `j = j->next`; otherwise the loop never ends.

check.q: What does a loop update like `j->next` (without `=`) do?
check.a: Nothing useful — it reads the pointer and discards it, so `j` never changes.

files.title: Insertion sort on a linked list (practice)
files.what: Sorts a singly linked list by moving the nodes themselves instead of swapping values. A second list is kept sorted at all times, and every node of the given list is dropped into its place inside it.
steps: Make a fake node `dummy` in front of the sorted list, so there is always a node to hang the next one from - even when the new value is the smallest so far.
Take the nodes of the given list one by one. Save `cur->next` first: the next line changes `cur->next` and the rest of the list would be lost.
Walk the sorted list from `dummy` while `p->next->val <= cur->val`. You stop at the node *before* the spot, because in a singly list only that node can be made to point at `cur`.
Hook `cur` in: `cur->next = p->next; p->next = cur;`.
Return `dummy->next`, one step past the fake node.
files.complexity: Time O(n²) in the worst case (each node may scan the whole sorted part) · Space O(1) - no new node is made for the answer
files.input_note: A count, then that many values; repeated until the input ends, so two lists are sorted in one run.
files.output_note: `1 2 3 4` and `-1 0 3 4 5` - the second line shows negative values are handled too.
files.watch_out: This is the opposite of the module's selection sort, which swapped `i->val` and `j->val` and left the nodes where they were. Here the nodes move, so `cur->next` must be saved before it is overwritten, and the walk must stop one node early.

check.q: Why does the search loop test `p->next->val` and not `p->val`?
check.a: Because `cur` has to be linked in by the node before it, so the walk must stop while `p` is still that earlier node.

practice_links.name: Remove Nth Node From End of List
Delete Node in a Linked List

recap: Delete in three moves: save the node, relink around it, `delete` it.
To delete index `idx`, stop at `idx-1`; index 0 is the special head case.
Deleting the tail of a singly list is O(n) — you need the node before it.
Selection sort on a list: two node pointers, swap `val`s, O(n²).
Always set a new node's `next` to `NULL`, and always move loop pointers with `p = p->next`.

check_yourself.q: Which deletions in a singly linked list are O(1), and which are O(n)?
check_yourself.a: Deleting the head is O(1); deleting the tail or any middle index is O(n) because you must walk to the previous node.

check_yourself.q: What two edge cases should a safe `delete_at_any_position` check?
check_yourself.a: Index 0 (use head deletion) and an index that is past the end of the list (do nothing).

check_yourself.q: Why can we sort a linked list without changing any `next` pointers?
check_yourself.a: Swapping the stored values reorders the data while the chain of nodes stays the same.

body: You can already build a list and add to it. This module is about taking something out of it, and that turns out to be the fiddly direction.
Picture a treasure hunt. Each card holds a prize and the address of the next card, and you are only told where the first card is. That is exactly a singly linked list.

Now someone says: drop the card holding 30 out of the hunt. Tearing that card up is not enough. The card holding 20 still sends you to the address of the torn card, and the address of 40 was written on the card you tore up. The hunt is broken.
So the whole module is one sentence: **stand on the node one before the victim, bend its arrow past the victim, and only then free the box.** Three moves, always in that order.
Take the list `10 20 30 40` and remove index 2 (the 30). You stand on 20. Here is the chain after each move:
intro.snippet:
Node* del = tmp->next;        // 1. hold the victim
tmp->next = tmp->next->next;  // 2. bend the arrow
delete del;                   // 3. free the box

body: Why stand *one before*? Because the arrows only go forward. If you are standing on 30 there is no way back to 20, and 20 is the only node whose `next` has to change. This is new: until now a walk stopped **on** the node you cared about, here it stops one node **short** of it.

That is why the loop is `for(int i = 1; i < idx; i++) tmp = tmp->next;` and not `i <= idx`. With `idx = 2` it runs once, so `tmp` ends on index 1, the node holding 20. `delete_at_any_position.cpp` on this page does exactly that.

**Three places, three different jobs.** Removing the head is the easy one: there is no node before it, so nothing has to be bent. Save the old head, move `head = head->next`, free the saved node. One step, however long the list is. But `head` itself changes, so the function must take `Node* &head`; with a plain copy, `main` would be left pointing at a freed box.
Removing a node in the middle is the walk above: as many steps as the index.

Removing the tail looks like it should be cheap, because you keep a `tail` pointer. It is not. You need the node *before* the tail, and no arrow points backwards, so you start at the head and walk until `tmp->next == tail`. A list of 1000 nodes costs 999 steps to drop the last one. That is O(n), and it is the one real weakness of this shape of list — Module 9 fixes it.
intro.trace:
delete head   [10]->[20]->[30]   1 step
delete idx 2  walk 1, then bend   idx steps
delete tail   walk to 30, cut     n-1 steps

body: **The mistake worth seeing once.** Suppose you free first: `delete tmp->next;` and then `tmp->next = tmp->next->next;`. The box is gone, and the address of 40 was written inside that box. You have thrown away the only note that said where the rest of the chain lives. What the second line reads now is freed memory: sometimes rubbish, sometimes a crash, and the 40 node is stranded with nothing pointing at it. Hold, bend, free.

**The second half of the page sorts a list.** Selection sort with two pointers: `i` walks the list, `j` walks everything after `i`, and whenever `j->val` is smaller you swap the two values. On `40 10 30 20` the first pass pulls 10 to the front, the next pulls 20 into second place, and you end with `10 20 30 40`. Note what is *not* happening: no `next` pointer is touched. The boxes stay put and only the numbers inside move, which is why the code is six lines instead of thirty.
The programs below take each delete on its own, then the sorts, then five practice problems. Several are broken on purpose, and the note under each says which line is wrong.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: deleting the 30 out of the middle
body: This is `delete_at_any_position(head, 2)` on the list `10 20 30 40`. Three moves, always in the same order: hold the victim, bend the arrow past it, free the box.

frames.label: The list is 10 20 30 40, counted from 0 at the head, and index 2 — the 30 — has to go.
`Node* tmp = head;`. As always, the walk begins at the only address you hold.

One hop, and `tmp` stands on 20, one box **before** the victim. Standing on 30 itself would be useless: from there you can see 40, but you can never see back to 20, and 20's arrow is the one that must change.
`Node* del = tmp->next;` writes down the victim's address. Do this first: after the next line nothing in the list points at that box, and a box you cannot find is a box you cannot free.
`tmp->next = tmp->next->next;` bends 20's arrow straight to 40. The 30 box is still in memory and still points at 40, but the list now steps over it, and only `del` knows where it is.
`delete del;` gives the box back to the heap. Hold, bend, free — in that order the list is correct at every moment in between.
frames.art:
tmp
head -> [10] -> [20] ---------> [40] -> NULL

        the 30 box has been freed

frames.label: Drawn straight: the list is 10 20 40. Nothing was shifted and no value was copied; one pointer changed and one box was freed.
Do it in the other order and the very next line has to read `next` out of memory you have already given away. It will often seem to work, which is the worst kind of bug.

wrong order: free first, then read

head -> [10] -> [20] -> [??] -> [40] -> NULL
                         ^ this box is gone, so
                           tmp->next->next is
                           anybody's guess
